Authorized permanent `forget` and every `open` reconcile them against canonical facts and report the outcome in `semantic_retrieval_posture()["derived_reconciliation"]` ... None of this is an erasure claim about rollback journals, backups, snapshots or the filesystem.
The system should not claim full deletion where it cannot demonstrate it.

L1.statement: After a governed deletion no version of the deleted generation is admitted to current or historical recall, nor by logical reference, and the owner's history reads tombstoned with no events, live and after restart.

L2.statement: The owner's re-creation is visible only as its own generation: old versions are withheld from recall, history (its whole payload) and write_semantics.

L3.statement: Another project's re-creation is isolated both ways: the former owner reads nothing of it and cannot write, correct, delete or dispute it (answering exactly as it would with no re-creation, except that a remember on an open id is the documented disclosure); the new generation reads nothing of the former.

L4.statement: Every deleted version is an as-of barrier for every reader, and a live generation resolves only for its owner, only from its own start.

L5.statement: A governed deletion of one superseded version withholds only that version, live and after restart; a deleted head or lineage member cannot be deleted again (already_deleted) and the attempt leaves the recorded tombstone (deleted_at, version, lineage) unchanged, live and after restart.

L6.statement: After a permanent deletion the canonical substrate holds no fact of the lineage, no public read of any scope serves an identifier or text of it, the derived-store reconciliation reports complete, and the owner still reads tombstoned. This is a claim about canonical facts and public reads only, not about rollback journals, WAL frames, backups, snapshots or the filesystem (docs/28: no full-deletion claim where it cannot be demonstrated).
